Triggerfish

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We follow the roller-coaster ride to success of Africa’s largest animation studio and go behind the scenes to the creators of award-winning characters that have thrilled audiences across the globe.

Unique Selling Point:
Triggerfish animation studio has produced two of the five highest-grossing South African feature films of all time - Adventures in Zambezia and Khumba - and, in collaboration with Magic Light Pictures, has animated five multi-award-winning BBC Christmas adaptations, including the Oscar-nominated Roald Dahl adaptation Revolting Rhymes, the Annecy-and-Kidscreen-winning Julia Donaldson adaptationStick Man, and the International Emmy-winning Zog.

Triggerfish is currently producing their third feature film, Seal Team, and Netflix’s first African animated TV series, Mama K's Team 4.

In 2013, the studio set up a non-profit organisation, the Triggerfish Foundation, with the mandate to create awareness about animation as a career in Africa, train future animators, and help them to make their first animation so that they would be employable, improving diversity and gender equality in the sector. Key initiatives include the pan-African Triggerfish Story Lab, supported by The Walt Disney Company; the all-women Triggerfish Writers Lab with Netflix; the free Triggerfish Academy digital learning platform; and regular bursaries to study at The Animation School.


Summary:
Triggerfish was established in 1996 as a stop-frame animation studio in Cape Town producing TV commercials and animation series for childrens’ programmes. The studio made their name with the popular Takalani Sesami and Sesami Street children’s series. In 2004, one of the junior animators on the series, Stuart Forrest, was made a partner together with Mike Buckland and Anthony Silverston.

In 2007, the company moved into computer-generated animation and shifted their focus to motion pictures. Adventures in Zambezia, and Khumba were their first two animation films. They pulled out all the stops, hired more people and worked to extreme deadlines to deliver the films for release in 2012/2013.

Forrest and the team were rewarded for their hard work. Both features were box-office successes and received several accolades, including Best Animation at South African Film and Television Awards and a Gold Panda Award for Best Foreign Animation film for Khumba.

But the next year, there was no work in the pipeline and no funding and salaries had to be paid. They nearly didn’t survive. 120 staff were retrenched, people they had nurtured for the past 10 years. It was a terribly difficult environment.

Two years later though, Triggerfish was back on track. Backed by global distributors, they made their mark again in the animation world. Over the last five years, they have thrived, creating a slate of award-winning films broadcasted on BBC One Christmas Specials and produced by Magic Light Pictures - a UK producer of children’s entertainment. These include Stickman, Revolting Rhymes, The Highway Rat, Zog and The Snail and the Whale.




Further information:
The Snail and the Whale premiered on BBC One at Christmas in 2019 to four-star reviews and over 7.5m viewers. Directed by multi-award winning South African director at Triggerfish, Daniel Snaddon, and two-time Oscar nominee, Max Lang, this is the story of a tiny snail with an itchy foot, who travels the world on the tail of a great big grey-blue humpback whale.

“For anyone who’s ever felt overwhelmed, like the world is too big for you to make a difference, The Snail and the Whale is an encouragement that even though you feel small, what you do still matters,” says Snaddon. “The important thing is to keep hoping and to keep trying.” Triggerfish themselves have faced tough times and kept going.

Zog, on the other hand, is the story of a dragon: the keenest, but clumsiest pupil in his class at Dragon School where he longs to win a gold star as he learns to fly, roar and breathe fire. Zog earned the keen-but-clumsy dragon a gold star everywhere, from Shanghai International TV Festival to New York International Children’s Film festival last year, as well as a nomination for International Emmy, Kidscreen, and Annie awards this year.

“This is some very welcome good news at a challenging time,” says Forrest. “The crew poured heart and soul into bringing Zog to life - a character that we all came to love - and to get one of the top TV prizes in the world is wonderful recognition for an incredible team.”

Now, Triggerfish has two more projects in production: Mama K’s Team 4 and Seal Team.

Mama K’s 4 Team is the first original African animated series for Netflix and is produced in collaboration with London-based kids’ entertainment specialists, CAKE. It tells the story of four teen girls living in the neo-futuristic African city of Lusaka, Zambia. The teens are recruited by a retired secret agent still committed to saving the world. Designed by Cameroonian artist, Malcolm Wope, it draws visual inspiration from retro-90s R&B and hip-hop girls’ groups. Wope is the lead character designer on Mama K’s Team 4 and a full-time employee at the Triggerfish studio in Cape Town.

“Triggerfish is delighted to bring Mama K’s Team 4 to life on Netflix,” says Vanessa Sinden, Triggerfish’s development producer. “And we are able to do this with the support of South Africa’s Industrial Development Corporation and the Department of Trade and Industry and CMG to finance the project,” says Sinden.

Drawing from local inspiration, Seal Team tells the story of an orphan seal who spends his days off the coast of South Africa eluding great whites until he decides to assemble a scratch team of like-minded seals to teach the sharks a lesson.

“To produce projects of this magnitude, many hours of animation are required,” says Sinden. “Besides our full-time staff count of 170 people here in South Africa, we draw on a pool of more than 160 freelance animators across the world - Paris, China, Dublin are some of the cities where they are remotely working from.”

“Unfortunately, there are simply not enough experienced animators locally, so part of our solution is to start growing our own talent and develop stories that originate here,” says Forrest. To this end, we established The Triggerfish Academy in 2019 - an online learning platform to encourage young minds to create their first animated film. We also provide bursaries to 13 talented youngsters to study animation,” says Forrest. The Academy is run in partnership with the Goethe Institute and the German Economic Federation and Development.

Storylab is another Triggerfish initiative under the guidance of development producer, Tendayi Nyeke. Her dream is to transfer skills and create employment in the creative field throughout Africa. With the help of the Department of Trade and Industry and Walt Disney Company, Storylab funding, she aims to uncover emerging African writers and directors. One of the 8 winners of the Triggerfish Story Lab initiative in 2015, was Zambian writer Malenga Mulendema for her Mama K’s Team 4 story.

“South Africa is making some of the best animation anywhere and we’re ready to take Africa’s stories to the world,” enthuses Forrest.

__________________________________________________________________________

The story
The story takes us through the highs and lows of Africa’s largest award-winning animation studio: Triggerfish. From their humble beginnings in 1997 to being on top of their game in 2013, Triggerfish have earned their stripes delivering award-winning animation films. Why were they struggling when their films were box office hits? We delve into the reasons and how they build themselves back up again in such a short period of time.

Except for the one-on-one interview with Nyeke in Johannesburg (she is currently still working remotely), the rest will be done here in the Cape Town studio via Zoom with the presenter. Strict safety regulations and social distancing will be adhered to.

All video clips of their animation films will be supplied by Triggerfish. With some of the employees still working remotely, a few shots of the 2013 Carte Blanche insert will be used to show a ‘busy’ studio environment.

Interviews
Stuart Forrest: CEO Triggerfish
Stuart Forrest is CEO of Triggerfish and producer of the continent’s two most commercially successful animation films, Khumba and Adventures in Zambezia. Forrest joined Triggerfish as a junior animator in 2002 to work on Takalani Sesame for seasons two and three, and became a partner in 2004. He was also one of the founders of AnimationSA, the official industry body in South Africa.

Tendai Nyeke: Content Producer
Nyeke's experience in broadcasting spans 15 years. As a commissioning editor at the SABC, her commissioned work received South African Film and Television Awards (SAFTA) in the genres of comedy, talk shows, game show and reality programming. A former Writer’s Guild of SA council member, she has worked as a development executive on multiple SAFTA-nominated shows and has written, produced and directed television programs across South Africa’s major broadcasters. She was the format co-developer of popular reality programme Our Perfect Wedding, which has been adapted across Africa. Passionate about where art and business meet, Nyeke holds an MBA in Music and Creative Industries from Henley Business School.

Daniel Snaddon: Director
Daniel Snaddon has co-directed three much-loved Julia Donaldson and Axel Scheffler adaptations: the 2020 International Emmy-winning Zog, the 2020 British Animation Awards winner The Snail and the Whale, and the BAFTA-nominated and Annecy-winning Stick Man. Snaddon was the founding director of Kunjanimation, which grew into CTIAF.

Vanessa Sinden: Development Producer
Sinden is producing Mama K’s Team 4 for Triggerfish, and also produced the pan-African Triggerfish Story Lab that unearthed the project, as well as Triggerfish’s first two films, Adventures in Zambezia and Khumba, which are two of the five highest grossing African films of all time. She’s also the founder of African Women In Animation, something she’s passionate about; mentors young talent through the Berlinale Durban Talents Mentor program; and is a producer on Triggerfish’s upcoming third feature, Seal Team.

Malcom Wope: Lead character designer and animator
Wope is the lead character designer on the Triggerfish project, Mama K’s Team 4, recently announced as Netflix’s first original African animated series, as well as Triggerfish’s third feature film, Seal Team. He was born in Yaoundé, Cameroon and moved to South Africa at age eight. He has a degree in architecture from The University of Cape Town, but would fill his architectural drawings with characters, to the degree that his lecturer suggested he was in the wrong industry. After graduating, he worked at Supa Strikas, first as an illustrator for the comic and then as a storyboarder for the hit TV series, broadcast on Disney XD in over 130 territories. He’s since worked on mobile, casino and AAA games he can’t speak about yet. He’s also the creator of Kung Fu Is Dead, an animated series that fuses martial arts and hip hop, and is currently in development with Triggerfish.

Script:


FINAL SCRIPT: Triggerfish
Duration: 8 minutes

V/O Meet Zog, a clumsy dragon who meets a princess and wants to learn to fly and blow fire.

Up sound

V/O Zog has a wish: To earn a golden star from dragon school.

Up sound

V/O For the artists who dreamt up Zog, it has been a big year. Up against animated films from France, Brazil and India in this year’s selection at the International Emmy Kids Award for animation, it was Zog who walked away with the honours.

Up sound

V/O. With the world in lockdown, the news was announced online by the panel on the academy’s website on 31 March 2020. The producers of Zog, Magic Light Pictures in the UK and Triggerfish in Cape Town, were delighted.

Up sound announcement

Up sound: “We would like to invite everyone that has worked on this film led by a brilliant director Max Lang and Daniel Snaddon, the whole crew at Triggerfish animation in Cape Town and all our teams here in London.”

V/O From Los Angeles to London and Shanghai, Triggerfish has in the last few years become the byword for award-winning, cutting edge animation craft. CEO Stuart Forrest started as a junior animator 17 years ago.

Stuart Forrest: CEO TRIGGERFISH - In 2003 there were probably 6 to 10 people depending how busy it was. Mostly it was Sesame Street we were doing; we did a couple of commercials but very small.

V/O In 2004, Forrest bought a share in the company but realised the company was in financial trouble.

Stuart Forrest: We started making Sesame Street animation in my kitchen. We did not tell them. We carried on at home a bit.

V/O After years of borrowing money to pay salaries, Forrest persuaded investors to take a big risk. The team had a story for a feature film they called Adventures in Zambezia. The investors took the leap with them. In two months, Triggerfish grew from 8 to 80 artists, hand-picking the best talent in the country; Vanessa Sinden came on board.

Vanessa Sinden: Development Producer - It is an amazing film. It just really represented these birds coming together and learning from one another and that is what the experience of making the film was like.

V/O Coasting on the momentum of Zambezia a second film soon followed. Daniel Snaddon was the animation lead on Khumba.

Daniel Snaddon: Director - For us on Khumba we could just concentrate on the creative and there were some technical challenges to overcome but my memories were of having a really good time.

V/O Both features excelled their wildest projections. Nine million cinema tickets were sold globally. It was dubbed into 27 languages and raked in $76m.

Up sound

V/O But the glory was short lived. The team had no immediate new projects lined up….and 80 salaries to pay.

Stuart Forrest: After Khumba we had nothing lined up. We had to go back to 5 people and let everyone go. We had to borrow money to keep alive.

V/O Forrest reached out to Magic Light Pictures, a UK-based film company they had been collaborating with here and there for some years, to market their joint services to the industry. The co-producers received their first order to animate Stick Man - a short film for the BBC’s Christmas special. Snaddon co-directed.

Up sound

Daniel Snaddon: We learnt pretty much what the British style of animation TV special making is and it is all about the quality and it is push, push, push the quality.

Claire Mawisa: Yes you won an award, an Annecy award.

Daniel Snaddon: We won best overall TV production at the Annecy International Animation Festival. It was a huge affirmation for the team that BBC and Magic Light Pictures trusted us with this property.

Up sound

V/O The partnership was set for greatness - their animation of legendary children’s author Roald Dahl’s Revolting Rhymes won 8 international awards including an Emmy and a BAFTA.

Up sound

Stuart Forrest: We have won Emmys, we have been nominated for an oscar and those accolades make a massive difference when you are talking to the next person. Our big problem now is we don't have enough people now and so we have to work really hard at growing the industry around us.

V/O Setting out to re-imagine the very industry they depend on, Triggerfish created free online courses for young talent to try their hand at animation and they provided funding for bursaries for promising students to attend South Africa’s two animation schools.

Daniel Snaddon: I think there is a type of person who gets such a huge kick out of seeing an image come to life and seeing a story play out and characters who are thinking and their way through these stories.

Up sound

V/O Triggerfish’s success had proven that the world was hungry for stories from Africa. In 2015, Storylab partnered with the Department of Trade and Industry and Disney. Their mission - to coach black female writers and directors to pitch their own story ideas to the world.

Vanessa Sinden: The Storylab was pitched to creators to take their ideas to partner them with opportunity, with amazing script gurus in Los Angeles, Disney execs from London and actually bring those projects to life.

V/O Zambian writer Malenga Mulendema was one of the 8 winners to be taken forward by Storylab. Her Mama K’s Team 4 became the first Netflix original animation series from Africa - produced by Triggerfish and Uk-based entertainment company CAKE.

Vanessa Sinden: This is the first project I have worked on where I had an all female writing room, all from the continent, so it is really exciting to see that shift.

Up sound

V/O Mama K’s Team 4 are superheroes that the world has been waiting for - four African schoolgirls from a neo-futuristic African city of Lusaka Zambia. Team 4 is recruited by a retired secret agent to save the world.

Malcolm Wope: Lead character designer and animator - The show is based in Lusaka, Zambia and Triggerfish sent us there just to get a feeling for the environment and the people there and a lot of that we used to put into the characters that we get on script.

V/O Designed by Cameroonian artist Malcolm Wope the Team 4 series is action-packed. Wope draws his visual inspiration from retro-90s R&B and hip-hop girls’ groups.

Malcolm Wope: My style is quite unique and action heavy and I was brought in to do a little bit of art for Mama K’s Team 4 and yeh, the style and the show meshed quite well together.

V/O Drawing on inspiration closer to home Triggerfish is now in production on Seal Team, another full length feature about an orphan seal that teaches the sharks a lesson. Newest member of Triggerfish Tendayi Nyeke, was brought in to grow local stories.

Claire Mawisa: How important is it to tell African stories?

Tendayi Nyeke: Development Executive - It is vital. When you look at the rest of the world they captured history in those stories. Where is the african history? And so I think africans must commit to capturing our identity, our history and animation is a timeless way to do it. I would love to see more of that happening to mastering that craft so that our history can be captured through this medium.

Up sound

V/O Triggerfish is celebrating its 24th birthday this year and from difficult roots it’s grown into a truly global company with staff in Paris, Dublin, China and Los Angeles.

Claire Mawisa: It is really inspiring to listen to you speak, knowing you were once working from your kitchen.

Stuart Forrest: Every now and then we can really look back and realise how far we have come.

_______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________


Promo 1:
Triggerfish: a small low-budget commercial and stop frame company in Cape Town, is today an award-winning producer of children’s animation films, watched by millions across the globe.

Promo 2:
The story of Triggerfish reads like a grim fable: From liquidation to bringing home the Emmys, they have become masters of their craft, rubbing shoulders with Disney and Pixar.

Promo 3
Triggerfish is no ordinary company - they have been liquidated, and faced hard times but have never lost sight of their dreams, and today they are Africa's most successful platform for creative excellence.

Up sound V/O Zog has a wish: To earn a golden star from dragon school. Up sound V/O For the artists who dreamt up Zog, it has been a big year. Up against animated films from France, Brazil and India in this year’s selection at the International Emmy Kids Award for animation, it was Zog who walked away with the honours. Up sound V/O. With the world in lockdown, the news was announced online by the panel on the academy’s website on 31 March 2020. The producers of Zog, Magic Light Pictures in the UK and Triggerfish in Cape Town, were delighted. Up sound announcement Up sound: “We would like to invite everyone that has worked on this film led by a brilliant director Max Lang and Daniel Snaddon, the whole crew at Triggerfish animation in Cape Town and all our teams here in London.” V/O From Los Angeles to London and Shanghai, Triggerfish has in the last few years become the byword for award-winning, cutting edge animation craft. CEO Stuart Forrest started as a junior animator 17 years ago. Stuart Forrest: CEO TRIGGERFISH - In 2003 there were probably 6 to 10 people depending how busy it was. Mostly it was Sesame Street we were doing; we did a couple of commercials but very small. V/O In 2004, Forrest bought a share in the company but realised the company was in financial trouble. Stuart Forrest: We started making Sesame Street animation in my kitchen. We did not tell them. We carried on at home a bit. V/O After years of borrowing money to pay salaries, Forrest persuaded investors to take a big risk. The team had a story for a feature film they called Adventures in Zambezia. The investors took the leap with them. In two months, Triggerfish grew from 8 to 80 artists, hand-picking the best talent in the country; Vanessa Sinden came on board. Vanessa Sinden: Development Producer - It is an amazing film. It just really represented these birds coming together and learning from one another and that is what the experience of making the film was like. V/O Coasting on the momentum of Zambezia a second film soon followed. Daniel Snaddon was the animation lead on Khumba. Daniel Snaddon: Director - For us on Khumba we could just concentrate on the creative and there were some technical challenges to overcome but my memories were of having a really good time. V/O Both features excelled their wildest projections. Nine million cinema tickets were sold globally. It was dubbed into 27 languages and raked in $76m. Up sound V/O But the glory was short lived. The team had no immediate new projects lined up….and 80 salaries to pay. Stuart Forrest: After Khumba we had nothing lined up. We had to go back to 5 people and let everyone go. We had to borrow money to keep alive. V/O Forrest reached out to Magic Light Pictures, a UK-based film company they had been collaborating with here and there for some years, to market their joint services to the industry. The co-producers received their first order to animate Stick Man - a short film for the BBC’s Christmas special. Snaddon co-directed. Up sound Daniel Snaddon: We learnt pretty much what the British style of animation TV special making is and it is all about the quality and it is push, push, push the quality. Claire Mawisa: Yes you won an award, an Annecy award. Daniel Snaddon: We won best overall TV production at the Annecy International Animation Festival. It was a huge affirmation for the team that BBC and Magic Light Pictures trusted us with this property. Up sound V/O The partnership was set for greatness - their animation of legendary children’s author Roald Dahl’s Revolting Rhymes won 8 international awards including an Emmy and a BAFTA. Up sound Stuart Forrest: We have won Emmys, we have been nominated for an oscar and those accolades make a massive difference when you are talking to the next person. Our big problem now is we don't have enough people now and so we have to work really hard at growing the industry around us. V/O Setting out to re-imagine the very industry they depend on, Triggerfish created free online courses for young talent to try their hand at animation and they provided funding for bursaries for promising students to attend South Africa’s two animation schools. Daniel Snaddon: I think there is a type of person who gets such a huge kick out of seeing an image come to life and seeing a story play out and characters who are thinking and their way through these stories. Up sound V/O Triggerfish’s success had proven that the world was hungry for stories from Africa. In 2015, Storylab partnered with the Department of Trade and Industry and Disney. Their mission - to coach black female writers and directors to pitch their own story ideas to the world. Vanessa Sinden: The Storylab was pitched to creators to take their ideas to partner them with opportunity, with amazing script gurus in Los Angeles, Disney execs from London and actually bring those projects to life. V/O Zambian writer Malenga Mulendema was one of the 8 winners to be taken forward by Storylab. Her Mama K’s Team 4 became the first Netflix original animation series from Africa - produced by Triggerfish and Uk-based entertainment company CAKE. Vanessa Sinden: This is the first project I have worked on where I had an all female writing room, all from the continent, so it is really exciting to see that shift. Up sound V/O Mama K’s Team 4 are superheroes that the world has been waiting for - four African schoolgirls from a neo-futuristic African city of Lusaka Zambia. Team 4 is recruited by a retired secret agent to save the world. Malcolm Wope: Lead character designer and animator - The show is based in Lusaka, Zambia and Triggerfish sent us there just to get a feeling for the environment and the people there and a lot of that we used to put into the characters that we get on script. V/O Designed by Cameroonian artist Malcolm Wope the Team 4 series is action-packed. Wope draws his visual inspiration from retro-90s R&B and hip-hop girls’ groups. Malcolm Wope: My style is quite unique and action heavy and I was brought in to do a little bit of art for Mama K’s Team 4 and yeh, the style and the show meshed quite well together. V/O Drawing on inspiration closer to home Triggerfish is now in production on Seal Team, another full length feature about an orphan seal that teaches the sharks a lesson. Newest member of Triggerfish Tendayi Nyeke, was brought in to grow local stories. Claire Mawisa: How important is it to tell African stories? Tendayi Nyeke: Development Executive - It is vital. When you look at the rest of the world they captured history in those stories. Where is the african history? And so I think africans must commit to capturing our identity, our history and animation is a timeless way to do it. I would love to see more of that happening to mastering that craft so that our history can be captured through this medium. Up sound V/O Triggerfish is celebrating its 24th birthday this year and from difficult roots it’s grown into a truly global company with staff in Paris, Dublin, China and Los Angeles. Claire Mawisa: It is really inspiring to listen to you speak, knowing you were once working from your kitchen. Stuart Forrest: Every now and then we can really look back and realise how far we have come. _______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo 1: Triggerfish: a small low-budget commercial and stop frame company in Cape Town, is today an award-winning producer of children’s animation films, watched by millions across the globe. Promo 2: The story of Triggerfish reads like a grim fable: From liquidation to bringing home the Emmys, they have become masters of their craft, rubbing shoulders with Disney and Pixar. Promo 3 Triggerfish is no ordinary company - they have been liquidated, and faced hard times but have never lost sight of their dreams, and today they are Africa's most successful platform for creative excellence. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We follow the roller-coaster ride to success of Africa’s largest animation studio and go behind the scenes to the creators of award-winning characters that have thrilled audiences across the globe.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Triggerfish animation studio has produced two of the five highest-grossing South African feature films of all time - Adventures in Zambezia and Khumba - and, in collaboration with Magic Light Pictures, has animated five multi-award-winning BBC Christmas adaptations, including the Oscar-nominated Roald Dahl adaptation Revolting Rhymes, the Annecy-and-Kidscreen-winning Julia Donaldson adaptationStick Man, and the International Emmy-winning Zog. Triggerfish is currently producing their third feature film, Seal Team, and Netflix’s first African animated TV series, Mama K's Team 4. In 2013, the studio set up a non-profit organisation, the Triggerfish Foundation, with the mandate to create awareness about animation as a career in Africa, train future animators, and help them to make their first animation so that they would be employable, improving diversity and gender equality in the sector. Key initiatives include the pan-African Triggerfish Story Lab, supported by The Walt Disney Company; the all-women Triggerfish Writers Lab with Netflix; the free Triggerfish Academy digital learning platform; and regular bursaries to study at The Animation School.
metadata.Summary: Triggerfish was established in 1996 as a stop-frame animation studio in Cape Town producing TV commercials and animation series for childrens’ programmes. The studio made their name with the popular Takalani Sesami and Sesami Street children’s series. In 2004, one of the junior animators on the series, Stuart Forrest, was made a partner together with Mike Buckland and Anthony Silverston. In 2007, the company moved into computer-generated animation and shifted their focus to motion pictures. Adventures in Zambezia, and Khumba were their first two animation films. They pulled out all the stops, hired more people and worked to extreme deadlines to deliver the films for release in 2012/2013. Forrest and the team were rewarded for their hard work. Both features were box-office successes and received several accolades, including Best Animation at South African Film and Television Awards and a Gold Panda Award for Best Foreign Animation film for Khumba. But the next year, there was no work in the pipeline and no funding and salaries had to be paid. They nearly didn’t survive. 120 staff were retrenched, people they had nurtured for the past 10 years. It was a terribly difficult environment. Two years later though, Triggerfish was back on track. Backed by global distributors, they made their mark again in the animation world. Over the last five years, they have thrived, creating a slate of award-winning films broadcasted on BBC One Christmas Specials and produced by Magic Light Pictures - a UK producer of children’s entertainment. These include Stickman, Revolting Rhymes, The Highway Rat, Zog and The Snail and the Whale.
metadata.Further information: The Snail and the Whale premiered on BBC One at Christmas in 2019 to four-star reviews and over 7.5m viewers. Directed by multi-award winning South African director at Triggerfish, Daniel Snaddon, and two-time Oscar nominee, Max Lang, this is the story of a tiny snail with an itchy foot, who travels the world on the tail of a great big grey-blue humpback whale. “For anyone who’s ever felt overwhelmed, like the world is too big for you to make a difference, The Snail and the Whale is an encouragement that even though you feel small, what you do still matters,” says Snaddon. “The important thing is to keep hoping and to keep trying.” Triggerfish themselves have faced tough times and kept going. Zog, on the other hand, is the story of a dragon: the keenest, but clumsiest pupil in his class at Dragon School where he longs to win a gold star as he learns to fly, roar and breathe fire. Zog earned the keen-but-clumsy dragon a gold star everywhere, from Shanghai International TV Festival to New York International Children’s Film festival last year, as well as a nomination for International Emmy, Kidscreen, and Annie awards this year. “This is some very welcome good news at a challenging time,” says Forrest. “The crew poured heart and soul into bringing Zog to life - a character that we all came to love - and to get one of the top TV prizes in the world is wonderful recognition for an incredible team.” Now, Triggerfish has two more projects in production: Mama K’s Team 4 and Seal Team. Mama K’s 4 Team is the first original African animated series for Netflix and is produced in collaboration with London-based kids’ entertainment specialists, CAKE. It tells the story of four teen girls living in the neo-futuristic African city of Lusaka, Zambia. The teens are recruited by a retired secret agent still committed to saving the world. Designed by Cameroonian artist, Malcolm Wope, it draws visual inspiration from retro-90s R&B and hip-hop girls’ groups. Wope is the lead character designer on Mama K’s Team 4 and a full-time employee at the Triggerfish studio in Cape Town. “Triggerfish is delighted to bring Mama K’s Team 4 to life on Netflix,” says Vanessa Sinden, Triggerfish’s development producer. “And we are able to do this with the support of South Africa’s Industrial Development Corporation and the Department of Trade and Industry and CMG to finance the project,” says Sinden. Drawing from local inspiration, Seal Team tells the story of an orphan seal who spends his days off the coast of South Africa eluding great whites until he decides to assemble a scratch team of like-minded seals to teach the sharks a lesson. “To produce projects of this magnitude, many hours of animation are required,” says Sinden. “Besides our full-time staff count of 170 people here in South Africa, we draw on a pool of more than 160 freelance animators across the world - Paris, China, Dublin are some of the cities where they are remotely working from.” “Unfortunately, there are simply not enough experienced animators locally, so part of our solution is to start growing our own talent and develop stories that originate here,” says Forrest. To this end, we established The Triggerfish Academy in 2019 - an online learning platform to encourage young minds to create their first animated film. We also provide bursaries to 13 talented youngsters to study animation,” says Forrest. The Academy is run in partnership with the Goethe Institute and the German Economic Federation and Development. Storylab is another Triggerfish initiative under the guidance of development producer, Tendayi Nyeke. Her dream is to transfer skills and create employment in the creative field throughout Africa. With the help of the Department of Trade and Industry and Walt Disney Company, Storylab funding, she aims to uncover emerging African writers and directors. One of the 8 winners of the Triggerfish Story Lab initiative in 2015, was Zambian writer Malenga Mulendema for her Mama K’s Team 4 story. “South Africa is making some of the best animation anywhere and we’re ready to take Africa’s stories to the world,” enthuses Forrest. __________________________________________________________________________ The story The story takes us through the highs and lows of Africa’s largest award-winning animation studio: Triggerfish. From their humble beginnings in 1997 to being on top of their game in 2013, Triggerfish have earned their stripes delivering award-winning animation films. Why were they struggling when their films were box office hits? We delve into the reasons and how they build themselves back up again in such a short period of time. Except for the one-on-one interview with Nyeke in Johannesburg (she is currently still working remotely), the rest will be done here in the Cape Town studio via Zoom with the presenter. Strict safety regulations and social distancing will be adhered to. All video clips of their animation films will be supplied by Triggerfish. With some of the employees still working remotely, a few shots of the 2013 Carte Blanche insert will be used to show a ‘busy’ studio environment. Interviews Stuart Forrest: CEO Triggerfish Stuart Forrest is CEO of Triggerfish and producer of the continent’s two most commercially successful animation films, Khumba and Adventures in Zambezia. Forrest joined Triggerfish as a junior animator in 2002 to work on Takalani Sesame for seasons two and three, and became a partner in 2004. He was also one of the founders of AnimationSA, the official industry body in South Africa. Tendai Nyeke: Content Producer Nyeke's experience in broadcasting spans 15 years. As a commissioning editor at the SABC, her commissioned work received South African Film and Television Awards (SAFTA) in the genres of comedy, talk shows, game show and reality programming. A former Writer’s Guild of SA council member, she has worked as a development executive on multiple SAFTA-nominated shows and has written, produced and directed television programs across South Africa’s major broadcasters. She was the format co-developer of popular reality programme Our Perfect Wedding, which has been adapted across Africa. Passionate about where art and business meet, Nyeke holds an MBA in Music and Creative Industries from Henley Business School. Daniel Snaddon: Director Daniel Snaddon has co-directed three much-loved Julia Donaldson and Axel Scheffler adaptations: the 2020 International Emmy-winning Zog, the 2020 British Animation Awards winner The Snail and the Whale, and the BAFTA-nominated and Annecy-winning Stick Man. Snaddon was the founding director of Kunjanimation, which grew into CTIAF. She’s also the founder of African Women In Animation, something she’s passionate about; mentors young talent through the Berlinale Durban Talents Mentor program; and is a producer on Triggerfish’s upcoming third feature, Seal Team. Malcom Wope: Lead character designer and animator Wope is the lead character designer on the Triggerfish project, Mama K’s Team 4, recently announced as Netflix’s first original African animated series, as well as Triggerfish’s third feature film, Seal Team. He was born in Yaoundé, Cameroon and moved to South Africa at age eight. After graduating, he worked at Supa Strikas, first as an illustrator for the comic and then as a storyboarder for the hit TV series, broadcast on Disney XD in over 130 territories. He’s since worked on mobile, casino and AAA games he can’t speak about yet. He’s also the creator of Kung Fu Is Dead, an animated series that fuses martial arts and hip hop, and is currently in development with Triggerfish.
